interest: This file offers exceptional historical insight into the complex legal, economic, and human dilemmas facing Japanese Americans (Nisei) and Japanese resident aliens (Issei) during the Allied Occupation of Japan. It documents how families utilized legal strategies—such as intergenerational gift deeds to American-born children or declarations of intent to naturalize—to shelter ancestral property from the sweeping expropriations of the post-war Japanese agrarian reform (Owner-Farmer Establishment Special Measures Law) and extraordinary capital levies. The correspondence illuminates the stringent financial walls erected by SCAP and the U.S. Treasury, where strict foreign exchange controls prevented the remittance of yen assets to the United States for corporate interests, Japanese war brides, and returning migrants. Furthermore, the file reveals institutional confusion over the racial barriers to U.S. citizenship prior to the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, exemplified by American consular officials in Tokyo questioning how a Japanese-born woman could lawfully file a declaration of intention in a California state court.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.5211, covering November 1946 to December 1949) documents the legal, administrative, and economic conditions governing real property ownership and transfers in post-World War II Japan under the Allied Occupation. Central themes include the enforcement of U.S. Treasury blocking regulations (Executive Order 8389), SCAP's strict prohibition on converting Japanese yen assets into foreign exchange, and the impact of the Japanese Land Reform Law (Owner-Farmer Establishment Special Measures Law) on absentee landowners residing in the United States. Individual cases feature Japanese immigrants and Japanese Americans attempting to convey family land in Hiroshima, Fukuoka, and Kobe to U.S. citizen relatives or utilizing declarations of intent to naturalize to avert compulsory land reform sales and extraordinary taxation. The file also chronicles corporate efforts by American enterprises, notably Standard-Vacuum Oil Company, to survey and rehabilitate commercial assets, as well as inquiries from American servicemen seeking to liquidate the Japanese property of their Japanese spouses.

subfiles.about: The State Department explains that wartime blocking regulations and postal restrictions prohibit transferring Kobe hospital property from an alien mother to her American citizen son.
subfiles.from: Benedict M. English, Assistant to the Legal Adviser, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Responding to an inquiry from attorney I. Charles Rubin, Benedict M. English explains that under Treasury Department General Ruling No. 11 and Executive Order 8389, business transactions with persons in Japan are strictly prohibited. Furthermore, because correspondence is limited to personal and family matters, communications regarding property conveyances are barred. As the property owner is not a U.S. citizen, the State Department cannot intervene and suggests writing to the Civil Property Custodian in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Letter from Benedict M. English to I. Charles Rubin regarding property transfer in Kobe

subfiles.about: An attorney inquires about the legal procedure for transferring hospital property in Kobe from a Russian national mother to her American citizen son.
subfiles.from: I. Charles Rubin, Attorney at Law
subfiles.summary: Attorney I. Charles Rubin writes to the Secretary of State on behalf of an American citizen client in Los Angeles who brought his Russian national mother and aunt to the United States from Japan. The mother owns hospital real estate on Yamamoto Dori in Kobe and wishes to execute a gift deed to her son in return for his guarantee of lifetime support. Rubin asks what procedure must be followed under Allied occupation regulations to effectuate the transfer.
subfiles.title: Letter from I. Charles Rubin to Secretary of State regarding conveyance of Kobe hospital property

subfiles.about: Standard-Vacuum Oil Company reports on the number of American firms that previously registered their Japanese property holdings with the War Department.
subfiles.from: F. D. Tracy, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.summary: F. D. Tracy reports that inquiries revealed fifteen American companies had registered Japanese property holdings through the National Foreign Trade Council with the War Department's Civil Affairs Division during 1943–1944. He notes this figure represents the probable maximum number of firms with substantial interests, referencing criteria used by William Clayton for Europe. Tracy hopes this information will facilitate discussions allowing corporate representatives to travel to Japan to assess war damage.
subfiles.title: Letter from F. D. Tracy to E. S. Martin regarding American corporate property holdings in Japan
subfiles.to: E. S. Martin, Division of Economic Affairs for Japan & Korea, Department of State

subfiles.about: The State Department informs Standard-Vacuum Oil Company of forthcoming discussions regarding corporate property rehabilitation in Japan.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Edwin M. Martin acknowledges Tracy's letter of October 15 and apologizes for the delay, explaining he had been waiting for replies from Japan. He states that an encouraging cable was received and that internal government discussions are underway. The Department expects soon to discuss a program allowing companies with substantial interests in Japan to assume direct responsibility for the protection and rehabilitation of their properties.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to F. D. Tracy regarding rehabilitation of American corporate property in Japan
subfiles.to: F. D. Tracy, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company

subfiles.about: Attorney Rubin clarifies that his client's mother is already residing in the United States and not in Japan.
subfiles.from: I. Charles Rubin, Attorney at Law
subfiles.summary: I. Charles Rubin clarifies a factual misunderstanding in the Department's letter of December 12, explaining that his client's mother is not in Japan but is residing with her son in Los Angeles. Only the property itself is situated in Japan. Rubin notes that he is following the Department's suggestion to request additional information from the Office of the Civil Property Custodian in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Letter from I. Charles Rubin to Secretary of State clarifying residence of property owner
subfiles.to: Secretary of State (Attention: Benedict M. English)

subfiles.about: The State Department outlines Treasury licensing and Japanese legal requirements for transferring blocked real property between U.S. residents.
subfiles.from: Benedict M. English, Assistant to the Legal Adviser, Department of State
keywords: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
subfiles.summary: Benedict M. English acknowledges that the property owner resides in the United States but points out that under Executive Order 8389, a Treasury license must be obtained from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to transfer property in a blocked country. He advises that commercial mail with Japan is again permitted. However, because conveyancing formalities are governed by Japanese law, Rubin should consult legal counsel familiar with Japanese legal requirements.
subfiles.title: Letter from Benedict M. English to I. Charles Rubin regarding Treasury licensing for blocked property

subfiles.about: The Japanese American Citizens League inquires whether Japanese agrarian land reform laws apply to agricultural land owned by an American citizen.
subfiles.from: Mas Horiuchi, Office Manager, Japanese American Citizens League
subfiles.summary: Mas Horiuchi writes on behalf of Hiroshi Mito, a U.S. citizen living in Salt Lake City who inherited 15 tan (approximately four acres) of land containing a house, family graveyard, and farmland from his grandfather in Japan. Mito inquires whether post-war Japanese government condemnation of agricultural land applies to property owned by an American citizen absentee landlord. Horiuchi asks the State Department to clarify whether the Japanese government has the legal power to confiscate such holdings.
subfiles.title: Letter from Mas Horiuchi to Edward M. Martin regarding Japanese land reform and U.S. citizen landholder
subfiles.to: Edward M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: The State Department requests specific property details to refer Hiroshi Mito's land reform case to military authorities in Japan.
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Edwin M. Martin informs Horiuchi that the question of whether Japanese land reform laws apply to foreign-owned property is currently pending before Allied military government authorities in Japan. To expedite handling, he requests specific information regarding the exact location of Mito's property, the name in which title is registered in Japan, and the grandfather's name. Upon receipt, the Department will submit the matter to Occupation authorities for investigation and disposition.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edwin M. Martin to Mas Horiuchi regarding Japanese land reform policy
subfiles.to: Mas Horiuchi, Office Manager, Japanese American Citizens League

subfiles.about: An attorney inquires about procedures for a Japanese national in California to transfer Japanese real estate to his American citizen son.
subfiles.from: A. H. Brazil, Attorney at Law
subfiles.summary: Attorney A. H. Brazil writes on behalf of Toshio Kumaki, a Japanese citizen residing in Arroyo Grande, California, who owns a home and parcel of land in Funaki-mura, Hiroshima Prefecture. Kumaki wishes to transfer this real estate to his son, James Katsuya Kumaki, a U.S. citizen residing in Chicago. Brazil asks the Secretary of State for guidance on the proper procedure to complete the transaction under applicable regulations.
subfiles.title: Letter from A. H. Brazil to Secretary of State regarding property transfer by Toshio Kumaki
subfiles.to: Office of the Secretary of State

subfiles.about: The State Department warns that property transfers from Japanese subjects to U.S. citizens require SCAP approval and substantial justification due to tax immunities.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Acting Chief, Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman replies that liquidating Japanese property and transferring dollar proceeds is currently impossible due to Japan's lack of foreign exchange assets. If Kumaki desires to transfer title to real estate remaining in Japan, SCAP's specific approval is required. Because conveying title to a U.S. citizen confers Allied national status and immunity from Japanese extraordinary taxes, SCAP requires substantial justification, and the Department requests further details on the nature and purpose of the transaction.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to A. H. Brazil regarding restrictions on property transfers and tax immunities

subfiles.about: Attorney Brazil clarifies that Toshio Kumaki intends a gift transfer to his son and seeks to appoint his sister as property trustee in Japan.
subfiles.from: A. H. Brazil, Attorney at Law
subfiles.summary: A. H. Brazil clarifies that Toshio Kumaki does not wish to sell his Japanese property, but rather intends to convey legal and equitable title to his son James Katsuya Kumaki as an outright gift. To manage the property and collect rents, Kumaki plans to appoint his sister, Yayeko Sennichi of Hongo Machi, Hiroshima Prefecture, as trustee or managing agent. Brazil states that Kumaki wishes to withdraw completely from ownership once the transfer is approved.
subfiles.title: Letter from A. H. Brazil to Secretary of State detailing Kumaki property transfer and trustee appointment
subfiles.to: Office of the Secretary of State (Attention: Roswell H. Whitman)

subfiles.about: The State Department informs attorney Brazil that the Kumaki property inquiry has been forwarded to the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Acting Associate Chief, Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman acknowledges Brazil's letter of January 16, 1948 regarding Toshio Kumaki's request to transfer Japanese real estate to his son. He states that the Department has referred the inquiry to the Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan in Tokyo. The Department promises to communicate further with Brazil as soon as a reply is received from Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to A. H. Brazil regarding referral of Kumaki case to Tokyo

subfiles.about: The State Department transmits attorney Brazil's inquiry to USPOLAD Tokyo to determine SCAP's position on property transfers conferring Allied tax immunities.
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 22 transmits a copy of A. H. Brazil's letter of January 16, 1948 concerning Toshio Kumaki's proposed property transfer to his U.S. citizen son. The instruction notes that such a transfer requires SCAP approval and substantial justification because it confers United Nations national privileges, including immunities from extraordinary Japanese taxes. The Acting Political Adviser is requested to raise the case with GHQ SCAP and report SCAP's official stance.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 22 from Department of State to Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan regarding Kumaki case
subfiles.to: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo

subfiles.about: The State Department forwards Toshio Kumaki's power of attorney to Tokyo for delivery to his sister Yayeko Sennichi.
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: The Department of State forwards an executed power of attorney from Toshio Kumaki empowering his sister, Yayeko Sennichi, to negotiate the transfer of his property to his American citizen son. The memorandum requests that the U.S. Reparations Delegation in Tokyo deliver the document to Mrs. Sennichi provided no objections are perceived.
subfiles.title: Foreign Service Operations Memorandum from Department of State to U.S. Reparations Delegation, Tokyo

subfiles.about: USPOLAD Tokyo reports SCAP's legal ruling that transfers of agricultural land to foreign nationals do not exempt property from Japanese land reform acquisition.
subfiles.from: Acting Political Adviser, United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo (J. W. Burnett)
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 167 acknowledges Instruction No. 22 regarding Toshio Kumaki and relays an opinion dated May 16, 1947 from the GHQ SCAP Legal Section. The opinion states that transferring agricultural land from a Japanese national to a non-Japanese national after the enactment of the Owner-Farmer Establishment Special Measures Law does not exempt it from compulsory purchase by the Japanese Government. Reference is also made to Yokohama despatch No. 411 outlining SCAP's overarching policy on agrarian reform and U.S. citizens.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 167 from USPOLAD Tokyo on Japanese agrarian reform law and property transfers

subfiles.about: A Japanese resident of Los Angeles asks the State Department to arrange for his son in Japan to cultivate his agricultural acreage exempt from land reform limits.
subfiles.from: Kyuji Hozaki
subfiles.summary: Kyuji Hozaki thanks Visa Division Chief H. J. L'Heureux for previous correspondence regarding a proposed visit to Japan to see his son Hisakazu. He explains that he owns 9 tan (2.25 acres) of land in Nakatsu-mura, Fukuoka Prefecture, which his son desires to cultivate. Because post-war laws restrict maximum cultivation acreage, Hozaki asks the State Department to request that General MacArthur's headquarters arrange for his son to farm the entire property temporarily until it can be sold.
subfiles.title: Letter from Kyuji Hozaki to H. J. L'Heureux requesting SCAP intervention on agricultural land in Fukuoka
subfiles.to: H. J. L'Heureux, Chief, Visa Division, Department of State

subfiles.about: The State Department declines to intervene with SCAP concerning agricultural land administration under Japanese agrarian reform law.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Acting Chief, Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman replies to Kyuji Hozaki's letter, explaining that the Department of State cannot ask SCAP to intervene in land disposition under Japanese land reform law. He emphasizes that the administration and enforcement of agrarian reform laws are solely the responsibility of the Japanese Government. Whitman advises Hozaki that his son in Japan should contact the appropriate Japanese government agency directly.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to Kyuji Hozaki regarding Japanese administration of land reform

subfiles.about: The State Department confirms receipt and forwarding of Toshio Kumaki's power of attorney to the U.S. Reparations Delegation in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Francis E. Flaherty, Acting Assistant Chief, Division of Protective Services, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Francis E. Flaherty acknowledges A. H. Brazil's letter of May 24, 1948 enclosing Toshio Kumaki's power of attorney in favor of Yayeko Sennichi. He confirms that the Department has forwarded the document to the United States Reparations Delegation in Tokyo for delivery to Mrs. Sennichi if no objections arise. Flaherty promises to communicate further if additional information is received.
subfiles.title: Letter from Francis E. Flaherty to A. H. Brazil transmitting power of attorney to Tokyo

subfiles.about: Attorney Brazil submits an executed power of attorney from Toshio Kumaki to his sister in Japan.
subfiles.from: A. H. Brazil, Attorney at Law
subfiles.summary: Responding to the Department's suggestion of May 4, attorney A. H. Brazil encloses a duly executed power of attorney from Toshio Kumaki to his sister Yayeko Sennichi. Brazil expresses confidence that the instrument will provide Mrs. Sennichi with adequate authority to effect whatever property transfer can be accomplished under occupation regulations.
subfiles.title: Letter from A. H. Brazil to Roswell H. Whitman enclosing Toshio Kumaki's power of attorney
subfiles.to: Roswell H. Whitman, Acting Associate Chief, Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Internal routing slip transferring Alfred Thunelius's inquiry regarding Japanese property conversion to the Division of Financial Affairs.
subfiles.from: John C. Thornburg, Division of Protective Services
subfiles.summary: John C. Thornburg of the Division of Protective Services transmits an incoming letter from Alfred E. Thunelius, Jr. to the Division of Financial Affairs. The slip notes that Thunelius's inquiry concerns the disposal of property in Japan and is referred for appropriate action.
subfiles.title: Department of State Reference Slip from John C. Thornburg to Division of Financial Affairs

subfiles.about: An American veteran asks whether his Japanese wife can sell property in Japan and convert the proceeds into U.S. dollars.
subfiles.from: Alfred E. Thunelius, Jr.
subfiles.summary: Alfred E. Thunelius, Jr. writes to the State Department stating that he married a Japanese woman in August 1947 and brought her to the United States in January 1948. Stating that his wife owns property and money in Japan, and noting a acquaintance reported his Japanese wife successfully converted sale proceeds into American dollars, Thunelius asks whether his wife can sell her assets and convert the funds into dollars, and whether she must return to Japan in person to settle the transaction.
subfiles.title: Letter from Alfred E. Thunelius, Jr. to State Department inquiring about Japanese property sale and dollar conversion

subfiles.about: The State Department explains that Japan's lack of foreign exchange precludes converting the proceeds of Japanese property sales into dollars.
subfiles.from: Edward W. Doherty, Assistant Chief, Division of Financial Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Edward W. Doherty informs Thunelius that SCAP and Japanese regulations contain no mechanism to convert yen realized from property sales into foreign currencies because Japan possesses no foreign exchange reserves. While property may be sold, proceeds must remain in Japan as bank deposits or be used for permitted local expenditures. Doherty discounts the report Thunelius heard as lacking foundation, but offers to raise the matter with SCAP if specific transaction details can be provided.
subfiles.title: Letter from Edward W. Doherty to Alfred E. Thunelius regarding exchange restrictions and yen balances

subfiles.about: An internal note critiquing USPOLAD's response on the Kumaki property inquiry and recommending standard transfer procedures.
subfiles.from: Orvis J. McDiarmid
subfiles.summary: In a handwritten internal memorandum to Richard B. Parke, Orvis J. McDiarmid comments that USPOLAD's reply was not responsive to the Department's inquiry. He suggests advising the applicants to put through the transfer in the usual manner and observe the outcome.
subfiles.title: Internal State Department Memorandum from Orvis J. McDiarmid to Richard B. Parke on Kumaki case

subfiles.about: A brief clerical note instructing a Department clerk to retrieve a specific file.
subfiles.from: Unknown
subfiles.summary: A brief handwritten internal buck slip addressed to Mildred requesting that she retrieve file '1005. New. 11.' from the records.
subfiles.title: Internal State Department Note requesting file 1005

subfiles.about: The State Department relays SCAP's legal ruling that transferring agricultural land to an American citizen does not protect it from Japanese agrarian expropriation.
subfiles.from: Roswell H. Whitman, Acting Associate Chief, Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Roswell H. Whitman informs A. H. Brazil that USPOLAD reported a May 16, 1947 GHQ SCAP legal opinion ruling that transferring agricultural land to a foreign national after the Owner-Farmer Establishment Special Measures Law does not exempt it from Japanese government purchase. Questioning whether a title transfer would be effective, Whitman suggests Kumaki designate an agent via power of attorney if he still wishes to proceed, reminding him that SCAP requires substantial justification before approving any transfer.
subfiles.title: Letter from Roswell H. Whitman to A. H. Brazil explaining SCAP legal opinion on agrarian reform

subfiles.about: The Immigration and Naturalization Service certifies Haru Ito's declaration of intention to become a U.S. citizen to contest Japanese agrarian land reform expropriation.
subfiles.from: Watson B. Miller, Commissioner, Immigration and Naturalization Service, Department of Justice
subfiles.summary: Watson B. Miller informs the Secretary of State that Mrs. Haru Ito requested verification of her declaration of intention to become a U.S. citizen for transmission to the Agrarian Land Reform Committee in Kusu-cho, Mie Prefecture. The committee required this proof to support her objection to the public sale of her property as an absentee landowner. Miller certifies that Ito filed declaration No. 2015 in the Superior Court of Riverside County, California, on August 1, 1947.
subfiles.title: Letter from Watson B. Miller to Secretary of State regarding Haru Ito's declaration of intention

subfiles.about: Draft memorandum questioning the lawful basis for a Japanese subject to declare intention for U.S. citizenship and requesting a missing airgram on property policy.
subfiles.from: USPOLAD, Tokyo (George Bruner)
subfiles.summary: USPOLAD Tokyo acknowledges receipt of the Department's transmittal of Haru Ito's declaration of intention. The post notes that a search of Tokyo and Yokohama records failed to find the Department's circular airgram of May 16, 1947, and requests a copy. The memorandum also questions how Mrs. Ito, born in Japan and presumably a subject of the Emperor, could lawfully file a declaration of intention to become a U.S. citizen in a California court.
subfiles.title: Draft Operations Memorandum from USPOLAD Tokyo to Department of State regarding Haru Ito naturalization

subfiles.about: USPOLAD Tokyo inquires how Japanese subject Haru Ito filed for U.S. naturalization to challenge agrarian land reform expropriation.
subfiles.from: USPOLAD, Tokyo (George Bruner)
subfiles.summary: In a finalized operations memorandum, USPOLAD Tokyo acknowledges transmittal of Haru Ito's naturalization declaration intended to resist agrarian property expropriation in Mie Prefecture. The mission notes that the Department's circular airgram of May 16, 1947 was never received in Tokyo or Yokohama and requests a copy. Furthermore, it asks how Mrs. Ito, a Japanese subject born in Mie Prefecture, could lawfully file a declaration of intention to become an American citizen in the Superior Court of Riverside County.
subfiles.title: Operations Memorandum from USPOLAD Tokyo to Department of State regarding Haru Ito and land expropriation
